topic.title: Connected particles (tow-bars and pulleys) and the force on a pulley
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks over six questions, sat every Summer. This is one of the long questions every year, Q4, Q5 or Q6, and among the paper's hardest: Summer 2025 Q4 ran a force diagram, the acceleration, the tension and then the force on the pulley, whose final part was the least well-answered item on that paper; Summer 2022 Q5 ended with one block landing and the other rising freely; Summer 2021 Q4 and Summer 2023 Q4 began from a timing; and Summer 2019 Q5, Summer 2024 Q6 and Summer 2026 Q4 ended with the tow-bar breaking. Expect 10 to 13 marks, with the separate equations carrying the early marks and the pulley's resultant or the motion after the break separating the top grades.
mustMemorise: One light inextensible string over a smooth pulley: the same tension and the same acceleration for both bodies
Write F = ma for each body separately, in that body's own direction of motion, then add to remove T
A body moving horizontally: its weight and the normal reaction balance, so neither enters the equation
The force on a pulley is the resultant of the two tensions: 2T when the sections are parallel, T√2 at a right angle (2T cos(θ/2) with θ the angle between the sections)
After a string breaks or goes slack, or a tow-bar snaps, redraw each body and recompute its own acceleration: a block rising freely slows at 10 m/s²
The tension in a tow-bar comes from one vehicle's own equation, the trailer's or the car's, never from the whole system
onFormulaSheet: v = u + at, v² = u² + 2as, s = ut + ½at², s = ½(u + v)t (Unit 2 formula sheet, page 2)
notOnThisSpec: Connected bodies on an inclined plane, and a pulley at the top of a slope: the commonest A level configuration and not a CCEA one
Three or more connected bodies; strings with mass; pulleys with moment of inertia
F = μR and coefficients of friction
Impulse and momentum in connected systems, and the jerk when a string becomes taut
The tension varying along a heavy string

mustBeAbleTo: Draw a separate free-body diagram for each connected body, with the same tension on both
Say why one tension and one acceleration serve both bodies
Write an equation of motion for each body in its own direction of travel
Add the two equations to remove the tension and find the acceleration
Substitute back for the tension and check it in the equation not used
Find the force on a pulley as the resultant of the two tensions: 2T for parallel sections, T√2 at a right angle
Find the tension in a tow-bar from one vehicle's own equation
Redraw and recompute after a string breaks or goes slack, or a tow-bar snaps, including the distance a body travels afterwards
Find the acceleration from a timing or a speed before any force is known, then the tension and the unknown
Keep an unknown mass or resistance as a letter and let the working produce it, taking the tension from the vehicle whose mass is known
sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2, g = 10 m/s² on the front page. This is one of the long questions and among the paper's hardest. Summer 2025 Q4 was a force diagram (2), the acceleration (6), the tension (2) and the force on the pulley (2). Summer 2022 Q5 ran a diagram, the acceleration, the tension and the pulley force, then one block landed and the other rose freely. Summer 2021 Q4 and Summer 2023 Q4 gave a timing first, then the tension and an unknown friction or mass. Summer 2019 Q5, Summer 2024 Q6 and Summer 2026 Q4 were a car and trailer, the later two with an unknown mass or resistance to show, each ending with the tow-bar breaking. Schemes are written in MW and W, with marks for each correctly formed equation and follow-through applied throughout.
traps: The force on the pulley taken as 2T when the two string sections are not parallel — the least well-answered item on its paper (Summer 2025 Q4(iv))
An equation written for the whole system where one body alone was needed, or the car's motion used for the trailer (Summer 2019 Q5, Summer 2024 Q6)
Weights and masses mixed in the same equation (Summer 2025 Q4(ii))
The weight of a block on a horizontal table carried into its equation of motion (Summer 2025 Q4)
Different letters used for the two ends of one string, or the other body's mass written into one body's equation (Summer 2023 Q4)
The normal reaction missing from a block's diagram (Summer 2023 Q4)
The earlier acceleration, or +10, used for a block rising freely after the string goes slack (Summer 2022 Q5); the old acceleration kept after the tow-bar breaks (Summer 2019 Q5)
A value printed in a later part used in an earlier one, which scored zero, and a 'show that' verified by substitution, which is capped at two marks (Summer 2024 Q6)

workedExamples.stem:
Two blocks of masses 5 kg and 3 kg hang at the ends of a light inextensible string passing over a smooth fixed pulley. The system is released from rest.

(i) Calculate the acceleration of the blocks.
(ii) Calculate the tension in the string.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 230' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='230'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M130 22H270' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M134 22l8 -8M146 22l8 -8M158 22l8 -8M170 22l8 -8M182 22l8 -8M194 22l8 -8M206 22l8 -8M218 22l8 -8M230 22l8 -8M242 22l8 -8M254 22l8 -8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.9' stroke-opacity='0.5'/><path d='M200 22V30' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><circle cx='200' cy='70' r='40' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><circle cx='200' cy='70' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M160 70L160 160' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><rect x='128' y='160' width='64' height='50' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='160' y='190.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>5 kg</text><path d='M240 70L240 160' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><rect x='208' y='160' width='64' height='50' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='240' y='190.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>3 kg</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A pulley fixed to a ceiling with a 5 kilogram block hanging on the left-hand section of the string and a 3 kilogram block on the right.

steps.working: One light inextensible string over a smooth pulley, so the tension $T$ is the same throughout and both blocks have the same acceleration $a$.
steps.decision: Say this before anything else. It is what licences using one $T$ and one $a$ in two different equations, and examiners report equations that look guessed when it is left out.

options: Because the string is light and inextensible and the pulley is smooth
Because the two blocks have the same mass
Because the two blocks move in the same direction
whyMenu.explain: They move in opposite directions, and their masses differ. It is the string and the pulley that force one tension and one rate of change of speed.

steps.working:
$50 - T = 5a$
For the 5 kg block, with down as positive.
steps.decision: One body, one diagram, one equation. Take each block's own direction of travel as positive for that block, and the heavier one is going down.

steps.working:
$T - 30 = 3a$
For the 3 kg block, with up as positive.
steps.decision: The lighter block rises, so its resultant is the tension minus its weight. Write it underneath the first equation, ready to add.

steps.working:
Adding:
$20 = 8a$
$a = 2.5$ m/s²
steps.decision: Adding the two equations cancels $T$ without any algebra. This is the step worth naming: it is what makes the pair solvable quickly.

steps.working:
Substituting back: $T = 30 + 3 \times 2.5$
Check in the other equation: $50 - 37.5 = 5 \times 2.5$
So $T = 37.5$ N
steps.decision: Put $a$ back into either equation for $T$, then check it in the one you did not use. The check costs ten seconds and catches a sign slip.

twin.stem: Blocks of 9 kg and 6 kg hang at the ends of a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley. Calculate the acceleration of the blocks, in m/s². Take $g = 10$ m/s².

workedExamples.stem:
A block of mass 7 kg rests on a rough horizontal table. It is joined by a light inextensible string, passing over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table, to a block of mass 5 kg hanging freely. The friction on the block on the table is 14 N. The system is released from rest.

(i) Calculate the acceleration of the blocks.
(ii) Calculate the tension in the string.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 222' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='222'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='16' y='92' width='232' height='116' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.05'/><path d='M16 92H248V208' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><rect x='78' y='46' width='88' height='46' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='122' y='74.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>7 kg</text><circle cx='268' cy='83' r='14' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><circle cx='268' cy='83' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M268 83L248 104' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><path d='M166 69L268 69' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><path d='M282 83L282 142' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><rect x='254' y='142' width='56' height='46' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='282' y='170.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>5 kg</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A 7 kilogram block on a rough horizontal table, joined by a string running over a pulley at the table's edge to a 5 kilogram block hanging below.

steps.working:
$50 - T = 5a$
For the hanging block, with down as positive.
steps.decision: Take each body on its own. The hanging block's forces are its weight and the tension, and its direction of travel is downwards.

steps.working:
$T - 14 = 7a$
For the block on the table, along the table.
steps.decision: This block moves horizontally, so its weight and the normal reaction balance and play no part. The forces along its motion are the tension and the friction.

options: Because it moves horizontally, so the vertical forces on it balance
Because the weight of a block on a table is always zero
Because friction has already accounted for the weight
whyMenu.explain: Its weight and the normal reaction are equal and opposite, so they contribute nothing along the direction of motion. They still belong on the diagram.

steps.working:
Adding:
$36 = 12a$
$a = 3$ m/s²
steps.decision: The same trick: add the equations and $T$ disappears. Notice the two blocks move in different directions, and that is exactly why each needed its own equation.

steps.working:
Substituting: $T = 14 + 7 \times 3$
Check: $50 - 35 = 5 \times 3$
So $T = 35$ N
steps.decision: Substitute into either equation and check in the other. The tension is less than the hanging weight, which it must be if the block is accelerating downwards.

twin.stem: A 10 kg block on a smooth horizontal table is joined over a pulley at the edge to a 15 kg block hanging freely. Calculate the acceleration, in m/s². Take $g = 10$ m/s².

workedExamples.stem:
A block on a rough horizontal table is joined by a light inextensible string, passing over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table, to a block hanging freely. The tension in the string is 35 N. The string runs horizontally from the block to the pulley and then vertically down to the hanging block.

Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force the string exerts on the pulley.

Round to 2 decimal places.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 262' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='262'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M24 66L250 66' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-opacity='0.6'/><path d='M272 88L272 250' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-opacity='0.6'/><path d='M250 88L302 36' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><path d='M288 22l28 28' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='250' cy='88' r='22' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><circle cx='250' cy='88' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M250 88L154 88' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M154 88L164 83.8L164 92.2Z' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M250 88L250 184' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M250 184L245.8 174L254.2 174Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='146' y='93' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>35 N</text><text x='250' y='204' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>35 N</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A pulley at the corner of a table. One string section runs horizontally to the left and the other hangs straight down, and each pulls the pulley with 35 newtons along its own direction, drawn from the axle.

steps.working: Both sections of the string pull on the pulley with the same force, 35 N, each along its own direction: one horizontally, one vertically down.
steps.decision: The pulley feels one pull from each section. They are equal because it is one light string over a smooth pulley, but they point different ways, so they cannot simply be added.

options: Because the force on the pulley is the vector sum of the two pulls
Because the force on the pulley is always twice the tension
Because the force on the pulley is the difference of the two weights
whyMenu.explain: Doubling the tension is right only when the two sections are parallel. Here they are at a right angle, and doubling is exactly what most candidates did on the least well-answered part of the Summer 2025 paper.

steps.working:
The sections are at $90°$ to each other, so the two pulls make a square and the resultant is its diagonal.
$R^2 = 35^2 + 35^2$
Pythagoras on the two equal pulls.
steps.decision: Draw the two pulls before reaching for a formula. Equal sides at a right angle make a square, and Pythagoras gives its diagonal. This line is the method mark.

steps.working:
$R = 35\sqrt{2}$, pointing between the two sections at $45°$ to each.
$R = 49.50$ N
steps.decision: For the record, two equal pulls with an angle $\theta$ between the sections give $2T\cos\frac{\theta}{2}$: parallel sections have $\theta = 0°$, which gives $2T$, and a right angle gives $2T\cos 45° = T\sqrt{2}$. CCEA's arrangements only ever make those two.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $49.50$ N, at $45°$ to each section of the string

twin.stem: The tension in a string over a smooth pulley is 50 N and the two sections are at right angles. Calculate the magnitude of the force on the pulley, in newtons. Round to 2 decimal places.

workedExamples.stem:
A block on a rough horizontal table is joined by a light inextensible string, passing over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table, to a block hanging freely. The tension in the string is 42 N. The string runs horizontally from the block to the pulley and then vertically down to the hanging block.

Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force the string exerts on the pulley.

Round to 2 decimal places.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 262' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='262'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M24 66L250 66' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-opacity='0.6'/><path d='M272 88L272 250' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-opacity='0.6'/><path d='M250 88L302 36' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><path d='M288 22l28 28' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='250' cy='88' r='22' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><circle cx='250' cy='88' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M250 88L154 88' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M154 88L164 83.8L164 92.2Z' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M250 88L250 184' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M250 184L245.8 174L254.2 174Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='146' y='93' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>42 N</text><text x='250' y='204' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>42 N</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A pulley at the corner of a table. One string section runs horizontally to the left and the other hangs straight down, and each pulls the pulley with 42 newtons along its own direction, drawn from the axle.

steps.working: Both sections of the string pull on the pulley with the same force, 42 N, each along its own direction: one horizontally, one vertically down.
steps.decision: The pulley feels one pull from each section. They are equal because it is one light string over a smooth pulley, but they point different ways, so they cannot simply be added.

options: Because the force on the pulley is the vector sum of the two pulls
Because the force on the pulley is always twice the tension
Because the force on the pulley is the difference of the two weights
whyMenu.explain: Doubling the tension is right only when the two sections are parallel. Here they are at a right angle, and doubling is exactly what most candidates did on the least well-answered part of the Summer 2025 paper.

steps.working:
The sections are at $90°$ to each other, so the two pulls make a square and the resultant is its diagonal.
$R^2 = 42^2 + 42^2$
Pythagoras on the two equal pulls.
steps.decision: Draw the two pulls before reaching for a formula. Equal sides at a right angle make a square, and Pythagoras gives its diagonal. This line is the method mark.

steps.working:
$R = 42\sqrt{2}$, pointing between the two sections at $45°$ to each.
$R = 59.40$ N
steps.decision: For the record, two equal pulls with an angle $\theta$ between the sections give $2T\cos\frac{\theta}{2}$: parallel sections have $\theta = 0°$, which gives $2T$, and a right angle gives $2T\cos 45° = T\sqrt{2}$. CCEA's arrangements only ever make those two.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $59.40$ N, at $45°$ to each section of the string

workedExamples.stem:
A car of mass 1500 kg tows a trailer of mass 480 kg along a straight horizontal road by a light horizontal tow-bar. The driving force of the car's engine is 2766 N. The car meets a resistance of $k$ N for each kilogram of its mass, and the trailer $2k$ N for each kilogram of its mass. The car and trailer accelerate at 0.9 m/s².

(i) Show that $k = 0.4$.
(ii) Calculate the tension in the tow-bar.

When they are moving at 7.2 m/s, the tow-bar breaks.

(iii) Calculate the deceleration of the trailer.
(iv) Calculate the time the trailer takes to come to rest.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 104' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='104'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M8 86H392' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M12 94l8 -8M24 94l8 -8M36 94l8 -8M48 94l8 -8M60 94l8 -8M72 94l8 -8M84 94l8 -8M96 94l8 -8M108 94l8 -8M120 94l8 -8M132 94l8 -8M144 94l8 -8M156 94l8 -8M168 94l8 -8M180 94l8 -8M192 94l8 -8M204 94l8 -8M216 94l8 -8M228 94l8 -8M240 94l8 -8M252 94l8 -8M264 94l8 -8M276 94l8 -8M288 94l8 -8M300 94l8 -8M312 94l8 -8M324 94l8 -8M336 94l8 -8M348 94l8 -8M360 94l8 -8M372 94l8 -8M384 94l8 -8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.9' stroke-opacity='0.5'/><rect x='44' y='26' width='92' height='56' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='90' y='51' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>trailer</text><text x='90' y='69' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>480 kg</text><rect x='200' y='16' width='108' height='66' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='254' y='46' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>car</text><text x='254' y='64' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>1500 kg</text><path d='M136 60H200' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='3'/></g></svg>
figure.alt: A car of 1500 kilograms towing a trailer of 480 kilograms along a horizontal road by a tow-bar.

steps.working:
Car: $1500k$ N
Trailer: $480 \times 2k$, which is $960k$ N
The resistances, with $k$ kept as a letter.
steps.decision: Each resistance per kilogram belongs to one vehicle, so multiply by that vehicle's own mass. Keep $k$ as a letter: the working has to produce its value, not use it.

steps.working:
$2766 - 1500k - 960k = 1980 \times 0.9$
Both vehicles together, so the tow-bar's pull cancels.
steps.decision: Treat the car and trailer as one body. The tow-bar pulls the trailer forwards and the car backwards equally, so it does not appear, and $k$ is the only unknown.

options: Because the tow-bar's pull is internal to the pair, so it cancels
Because the tow-bar carries no tension while they accelerate
Because the trailer's resistance is too small to count
whyMenu.explain: The tension acts forwards on the trailer and backwards on the car. Taken together those cancel, which leaves one equation with only $k$ in it.

steps.decision: Collect the $k$ terms and solve. In a show-that this is the line that earns the mark: the value has come out of the working, not gone into it.

steps.working:
The trailer alone:
$T - 384 = 480 \times 0.9$
$T = 816$ N
steps.decision: With $k$ known, the trailer's resistance is $480 \times 0.8$, which is 384 N. The trailer's own equation now has one unknown, the tension.

options: Because the trailer's own equation now holds only one unknown
Because the car's equation cannot give the tension
Because the tension equals the trailer's resistance
whyMenu.explain: Either vehicle's own equation gives the tension. The car's gives the same: $2766 - 600 - T = 1500 \times 0.9$.

steps.working:
After the break, only the resistance acts along the road:
$384 = 480a$
Deceleration $= 0.8$ m/s²
steps.decision: With the tow-bar gone there is no tension, and the old acceleration no longer applies. The trailer's resistance is the only horizontal force on it, and it opposes the motion.

options: Because nothing pulls the trailer now, so only its resistance acts
Because it keeps the acceleration it had before the break
Because the car's driving force now acts backwards on it
whyMenu.explain: The 2019 report records the old acceleration kept after a tow-bar breaks. Redraw the trailer on its own: resistance backwards, and nothing forwards.

steps.decision: It comes to rest, so its final velocity is 0. With forwards positive, the deceleration enters as a negative acceleration.

twin.stem: A trailer of mass 360 kg is towed along a horizontal road with an acceleration of 1.5 m/s². The resistance to its motion is 200 N. Calculate the tension in the tow-bar, in newtons.

items.skill: Prerequisite: solving simultaneous equations by adding
items.stem: From an earlier topic: add $50 - T = 5a$ and $T - 30 = 3a$. What is left?

options.feedback: The $T$ terms cancel: $50 - 30 = 20$ and $5a + 3a = 8a$.
The two $a$ terms add, so the right-hand side is $8a$.
The left-hand sides give $50 - 30$, not $50 + 30$.
$-T$ and $+T$ cancel, so no $T$ survives.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a resultant force of 45 N acts on a body of mass 9 kg. What is its acceleration?

options.feedback: That multiplies instead of dividing.
The fraction is upside down.
That subtracts; $F = ma$ is a product.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: two equal lengths of 5 are at right angles. How long is the diagonal of the square they make?

options.feedback: That adds the two lengths. At a right angle they combine by Pythagoras.
That is the sum of the squares; the root is still to be taken.
That is one of the squares.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: what is the weight of a 12 kg block, taking $g = 10$ m/s²?

options.feedback: That is the mass with a newton sign on it.
That divides by $g$.
That adds $g$ rather than multiplying by it.

items.stem: Two blocks are joined by a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley. Which is true?

options.text: The tension is the same on both sections and the blocks have the same acceleration
options.feedback: A light string over a smooth pulley carries one tension, and an inextensible string forces one rate of change of speed.

options.text: Each block has its own tension, found from its own weight
options.feedback: That would need a heavy string or a rough pulley. Two different letters here is what the reports record going wrong.

options.text: The heavier block has the larger acceleration
options.feedback: The string ties them together, so they speed up at the same rate in opposite directions.

options.text: The tension equals the heavier block's weight
options.feedback: That would be true only if the heavier block hung still. It is accelerating downwards, so its weight must be larger than the tension.

items.stem: A 5 kg block hangs from a string and accelerates downwards. Which equation is right for that block?

options.feedback: Its own forces are its weight and the tension, and it is travelling downwards.
That takes up as the direction of travel, so the acceleration would come out negative.
The friction acts on the other block, not on this one. Each equation carries only its own body's forces.
That uses the whole system's mass in one body's equation.

items.skill: The force on a pulley, parallel sections
items.stem: Two blocks hang either side of a pulley and the tension is 40 N. What is the magnitude of the force on the pulley?

options.feedback: Both sections hang vertically, so the two pulls are parallel and add directly to $2T$.
That is one pull. The pulley feels both sections.
That is $40\sqrt{2}$, which is the answer when the sections are at a right angle, not parallel.
The two pulls point the same way, downwards, so they reinforce rather than cancel.

items.skill: The force on a pulley, sections at a right angle
items.stem: A string runs horizontally from a table, over a pulley at the edge, and vertically down. The tension is 40 N. What is the magnitude of the force on the pulley?

options.feedback: $40\sqrt{2} = 56.57$ N: the two equal pulls at a right angle make a square, and the resultant is its diagonal.
Doubling the tension is right only when the two sections are parallel. This is the substitution the reports call the least well-answered item on the paper.
That is one pull on its own.
Two pulls at a right angle cannot cancel; only two opposite pulls could.

items.skill: The pulley feels the tensions, not the weights
items.stem: A 5 kg block and a 3 kg block hang either side of a smooth pulley, and the tension in the string is 37.5 N. What is the magnitude of the force the string exerts on the pulley?

options.feedback: Both sections pull straight down with 37.5 N, so the resultant is $2 \times 37.5 = 75$ N. It is always the tensions that combine.
That adds the two weights, 50 N and 30 N. The pulley is pulled by the string, not by the blocks, and while they accelerate the tension equals neither weight.
That is one section's pull. The pulley is held by both sections, and here they pull the same way.
That is the out-of-balance force that accelerates the blocks, the difference of their weights. The force on the pulley is built from the two tensions.

items.stem: A tow-bar snaps while a car is towing a trailer. What happens to the trailer?

options.text: It becomes its own problem: no tension, so only the resistance acts and it decelerates
options.feedback: Redraw it on its own. The tension is gone, and whatever forces remain give it a new acceleration.

options.text: It keeps the acceleration it had before
options.feedback: The force that was pulling it forward has gone, so its acceleration cannot be the same.
It still has its speed; the resistance takes that speed away over time rather than at once.
It is on a horizontal road, so gravity is balanced by the ground.

items.skill: Mass against force in a connected equation
items.stem: A 7 kg block on a rough table is pulled by a string with tension $T$ against friction of 14 N. Which equation is right for that block?

options.feedback: The forces along its motion are the tension forward and the friction back, and the $m$ is the mass in kilograms.
Its weight acts downwards, at right angles to the motion, and the normal reaction balances it, so it has no part along the table. The Summer 2025 report names this equation shape as a frequent error.
That uses the weight where $F = ma$ wants the mass.
The friction is given in the stem and it opposes the motion, so it belongs in the equation.

items.skill: Each part uses only what is known at that point
items.stem: A car of known mass, driving force and resistance tows a trailer of unknown mass. Part (i) asks for the tension in the tow-bar; part (ii) says 'Show that the mass of the trailer is 600 kg'. How should part (i) be answered?

options.text: From the car's own equation of motion, which has only one unknown
options.feedback: Everything acting on the car is given, so its equation gives the tension straight away. The 600 kg belongs to part (ii) and is not yet yours to use.

options.text: From the trailer's equation, putting in 600 kg because the question prints it
options.feedback: A value printed in a later part may not be used in an earlier one. In Summer 2024 this exact substitution scored zero for the whole part.

options.text: From the whole system, with 600 kg added to the car's mass
options.feedback: That also borrows the printed 600 kg before it has been shown, and the whole system could never give the tension anyway: the tension is internal to the pair.

options.text: From the trailer's equation, with its mass left as a letter
options.feedback: The trailer's equation has two unknowns at this point, the tension and the mass, so on its own it cannot give either. The car's equation has only one.

The resultant is the weight minus the tension.
parts.workedSolution: Down positive: $40 - T = 4 \times 2$, so $T = 32$ N. The tension is less than the weight, because the block is speeding up downwards.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the tension if the block were still. It is accelerating downwards, so the weight wins: $40 - T = 4 \times 2$.

parts.stem:

scheme.for: $R^2 = 50^2 + 50^2$: the two pulls are at a right angle, so they combine by Pythagoras

hints: One section is horizontal and one is vertical.
Two equal pulls at a right angle make a square; the resultant is its diagonal.
parts.workedSolution: The two pulls are equal and at $90°$, so $R^2 = 50^2 + 50^2$ and $R = 50\sqrt{2} = 70.71$ N, at $45°$ to each section.

commonErrors.feedback: That doubles the tension, which is right only when the two sections are parallel. Here one is horizontal and one is vertical, so they combine by Pythagoras: $R^2 = 50^2 + 50^2$. Doubling was what most candidates did on the least well-answered part of the Summer 2025 paper.
That is one section's pull. Both sections press on the pulley, and at a right angle their resultant is larger than either.

parts.stem:

hints: You need the tension before you can find the force on the pulley, and the acceleration before the tension.
One section runs along the table and one hangs down: a right angle.
parts.workedSolution: Adding the two equations gives $20 = 5a$, so $a = 4$ m/s² and $T = 3 \times 4 = 12$ N. The sections are at a right angle, so $R^2 = 12^2 + 12^2$ and $R = 12\sqrt{2} = 16.97$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: The tension of 12 N is right, but doubling it assumes the two sections are parallel. One runs along the table and one hangs down, so the pulls are at a right angle and combine by Pythagoras.

The right-angle step is right, but the tension used is the hanging block's weight, 20 N. That would hold only if the block hung still; it is accelerating downwards, so the tension is less than its weight. Find $a$ first, then $T$.

context.setting: Choosing the right pulley result

parts.stem:
When is the force on a smooth pulley equal to twice the tension in the string?

Answer ________

options.text: Only when the two sections of string are parallel
options.feedback: Then the two pulls point the same way and add directly.

options.text: Always, whatever the angle between the sections
options.feedback: At a right angle the resultant is $T\sqrt{2}$, which is smaller than $2T$.

options.text: Only when the two sections are at a right angle
options.feedback: That is the $T\sqrt{2}$ case, not the $2T$ case.

options.text: Only when the two bodies have equal masses
options.feedback: Equal masses would mean no acceleration at all, and the geometry of the string is what decides the resultant.

scheme.for: only when the two sections are parallel

hints: The force on the pulley is the vector sum of the two pulls.
parts.workedSolution: The force on the pulley is the resultant of the two pulls, so it is $2T$ only when they point the same way, which means the sections are parallel.

parts.stem:

Calculate the acceleration of the blocks.

scheme.for: $T = 2a$ for the block on the table

hints: The table is smooth, so there is no friction on that block.
Its weight and the normal reaction balance, so they play no part.
parts.workedSolution: Adding the two equations gives $30 = 5a$, so $a = 6$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That divides the hanging weight by its own mass alone, which would be right only if the string were cut. The block on the table is being accelerated too.

That takes the weight of the block on the table, 20 N, off the driving force. Its weight acts downwards into the table, at right angles to its motion, and the table balances it, so it has no part in the motion along the table.

parts.stem:
A car of mass 1000 kg tows a trailer of mass 500 kg along a straight horizontal road. The car's engine provides a driving force of 4500 N, and each vehicle meets a resistance of 1 N for every kilogram of its mass. The car and trailer accelerate at 2 m/s².

Calculate the tension in the tow-bar.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: for the trailer: $T - 500 = 500 \times 2$, or the car's equation

hints: Use one vehicle on its own. For the trailer, the tow-bar and the resistance are the only forces along its motion.
Convert the per-kilogram resistance first.
parts.workedSolution: For the trailer: $T - 500 = 500 \times 2 = 1000$, so $T = 1500$ N. The car's equation, $4500 - 1000 - T = 1000 \times 2$, gives the same.

commonErrors.feedback: That writes the trailer's equation with the car's mass and the car's resistance in it. Each equation carries only its own body's numbers: for the trailer, $T - 500 = 500 \times 2$.
The 1 N per kilogram has been used as the whole resistance. The trailer is 500 kg, so its resistance is 500 N.

context.setting: A trailer after its tow-bar snaps

parts.stem:
A car of mass 1000 kg tows a trailer of mass 500 kg along a straight horizontal road, and the pair accelerate at 2 m/s². The resistance to the trailer's motion is 1 N per kg of its mass. The tow-bar snaps, and the resistance is unchanged.

Calculate the deceleration of the trailer immediately afterwards.

Answer ________ m/s²

scheme.for: the trailer is now on its own, with no tension acting

hints: Redraw the trailer on its own: which forces are left?
A deceleration is quoted as a positive size.
parts.workedSolution: With the tow-bar gone, only the resistance of 500 N acts along the trailer's motion, and it acts backwards: $-500 = 500a$, so $a = -1$ m/s² and the deceleration is $1$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That is the acceleration the pair had while they were joined. The tow-bar has gone, so the force that was driving the trailer forward has gone with it: redraw and start again.
That divides the trailer's resistance by the mass of both vehicles. The trailer is on its own now, so only its own mass appears.
Your working is right: with forwards positive, $a = -1$ m/s². The question asks for the deceleration, which is the size of that, so the answer is 1 m/s² with no minus sign.

Answer ________

options.text: Because the string is light and the pulley is smooth
options.feedback: A light string carries the same tension throughout, and a smooth pulley does not change it as the string passes over.

options.text: Because the two blocks have the same mass
options.feedback: They usually do not, and the tension would still be the same if they did.
That is what makes the two accelerations equal, which is a different fact worth stating separately.
The tension would be the same whether they accelerated or not.

scheme.for: the string is light and the pulley is smooth

hints: One reason is about the string's mass, the other about the pulley.
parts.workedSolution: A light string carries one tension throughout, and a smooth pulley does not change it, so both sections pull with the same force.

parts.stem:
Two blocks are joined by a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley.

Why do both blocks have the same magnitude of acceleration?

Answer ________

options.text: Because the string is inextensible, so it cannot stretch
options.feedback: One block can only move as fast as the string lets the other, so their speeds change together.
That is what makes the tension the same, which is a separate fact.
A smooth pulley keeps the tension unchanged; it says nothing about how fast the blocks move.

options.text: Because they have the same weight
options.feedback: They generally do not, and if they did neither would accelerate.

hints: Ask what would happen if the string could stretch.
parts.workedSolution: The string cannot stretch, so as one block moves the other must move by the same amount, and their speeds change at the same rate.

context.setting: A block still rising when the string breaks

parts.stem:
Two blocks hang at the ends of a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley, and they move with an acceleration of 2 m/s². The lighter block is moving upwards at 3 m/s when the string breaks.

Calculate how much higher the lighter block rises before it starts to fall.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: with the string gone the block is a free body under gravity, so $a = -10$

hints: Once the string breaks the only force on the block is its weight.
At the top of the rise the velocity is zero.
parts.workedSolution: With no tension the block is in free flight and only its weight acts, so, taking up as positive, $0 = 3^2 - 2(10)s$ and $s = 0.45$ m. The 2 m/s² belonged to the pair and ended with the string.

commonErrors.feedback: That uses the pair's 2 m/s², which belonged to the blocks while the string joined them. Once it breaks the block has only its weight acting, so it slows at $10$ m/s². The Summer 2022 report names exactly this reuse.
That divides $u^2$ by $10$ instead of by $2 \times 10$. From $0 = u^2 - 2gs$, $s = \frac{u^2}{2g} = \frac{9}{20}$.

parts.stem:
Block $A$, of mass 7 kg, rests on a rough horizontal table. A light inextensible string joins it, over a smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table, to block $B$, of mass 5 kg, which hangs freely. The friction acting on $A$ is 14 N. The system is released from rest.

Calculate the acceleration of the blocks.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: One equation for each block, in that block's own direction of motion.
$A$ moves horizontally, so its weight and the normal reaction balance.
Add the two equations to remove $T$.
parts.workedSolution: For $B$: $50 - T = 5a$. For $A$: $T - 14 = 7a$. Adding gives $36 = 12a$, so $a = 3$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That brings $A$'s weight, 70 N, into the equation of motion. $A$ moves horizontally, so its weight presses into the table and the normal reaction balances it: neither appears along the motion. The Summer 2025 report names this as a frequent error.
The friction has been dropped from the combined equation. It is given as 14 N and it opposes the motion, so it comes off the driving weight.
That divides by $B$'s mass alone. Both blocks are being accelerated by the same string, so the combined equation carries both masses.

parts.stem:
Calculate the tension in the string that joins the blocks.

Answer ________ N
hints: Substitute the acceleration into either block's equation.
Check it in the other one.
parts.workedSolution: For $A$: $T - 14 = 7 \times 3$, so $T = 35$ N. Checking with $B$: $50 - 35 = 15$, which is $5 \times 3$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $ma$ for $A$, with the friction left out: it sets the tension equal to the resultant. The tension has to overcome the 14 N of friction as well as accelerate the block.
That comes from $T - 50 = 5a$, which takes up as $B$'s direction of travel. $B$ is accelerating downwards, so its resultant is its weight minus the tension: $50 - T = 5a$.

parts.stem:
The string runs horizontally from $A$ to the pulley and then vertically down to $B$.

Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force the string exerts on the pulley.

Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: $R^2 = 35^2 + 35^2$: the two tensions act at a right angle

hints: Both sections pull on the pulley with the same force, the tension.
One section is horizontal and one is vertical, so draw the two pulls and find their resultant.
parts.workedSolution: Each section pulls the pulley with 35 N, one horizontally and one vertically, so $R^2 = 35^2 + 35^2$ and $R = 35\sqrt{2} = 49.50$ N, at $45°$ to each section.

commonErrors.feedback: That doubles the tension. $2T$ is right only when the two sections pull the same way; here one is horizontal and one is vertical, so the pulls combine by Pythagoras. Doubling was what most candidates did on the least well-answered part of the Summer 2025 paper.
That is one section's pull. The pulley is held by both, so their resultant is what it feels.
That adds the two weights. The pulley feels the string, not the blocks, so it is the tensions that combine.

Blocks $P$ and $Q$, of masses 5 kg and 3 kg, hang at the ends of a light inextensible string passing over a smooth fixed pulley. Both blocks are held at rest 0.8 m above a horizontal floor, and are then released.

Calculate the acceleration of the blocks.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: One equation for each block, with the same $T$ and the same $a$.
Add them so that $T$ cancels.
parts.workedSolution: For $P$: $50 - T = 5a$. For $Q$: $T - 30 = 3a$. Adding gives $20 = 8a$, so $a = 2.5$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That divides the out-of-balance weight by $P$'s mass alone. The string is accelerating both blocks, so both masses appear.
That works with masses in kilograms where the equation needs weights in newtons. The out-of-balance force is $20$ N.

parts.stem:
Calculate the tension in the string that joins the blocks.

Answer ________ N
hints: Substitute the acceleration into either equation, then check it in the other.
parts.workedSolution: For $Q$: $T - 30 = 3 \times 2.5$, so $T = 37.5$ N. Checking with $P$: $50 - 37.5 = 12.5$, which is $5 \times 2.5$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $ma$ for $Q$, which is its resultant, not the tension. The tension also has to hold $Q$'s weight of 30 N up: $T - 30 = 3a$.

parts.stem:
Both sections of the string hang vertically.

Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force the string exerts on the pulley.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: $2T$: the two pulls are parallel, so the resultant is their sum

hints: Both sections pull straight down on the pulley.
parts.workedSolution: Both sections pull down with 37.5 N, so the resultant is $2 \times 37.5 = 75$ N, downwards.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $T\sqrt{2}$, the right-angle case. Here both sections hang vertically, so the pulls are parallel and add to $2T$. The Summer 2022 report records many candidates not knowing this.
That adds the two blocks' weights. The pulley is held by the string, so it is the two tensions that combine, and while the blocks accelerate the tension equals neither weight.

parts.stem:
$P$ hits the floor and does not rebound.

Calculate the speed of $P$ just before it hits the floor.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: $P$ falls from rest through the height it was held at, with the acceleration from part (a).
Choose the formula without $t$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $v^2$. The last step is the square root: $v = \sqrt{4}$.

parts.stem:
When $P$ hits the floor the string goes slack. $Q$ keeps moving upwards and does not reach the pulley.

Calculate the greatest height of $Q$ above the floor.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: with the string slack $Q$ moves freely under gravity: $0 = 2^2 + 2(-10)s$

hints: Redraw $Q$ on its own: with the string slack, only its weight acts, so $a = -10$ with up positive.
By the time $P$ lands, $Q$ has already risen 0.8 m from where it started.
parts.workedSolution: With the string slack, $Q$ has only its weight acting, so, with up positive, $0 = 2^2 + 2(-10)s$ and $s = 0.2$ m. $Q$ started 0.8 m above the floor and rose 0.8 m while $P$ fell, so its greatest height is $0.8 + 0.8 + 0.2 = 1.8$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: That keeps the 2.5 m/s² the blocks had while the string was taut. Once it is slack, $Q$ is on its own and gravity alone slows it, at 10 m/s². The Summer 2022 report names this reuse.
That takes $a = +10$ for a block moving upwards, so the rise comes out negative. With up positive, gravity slows $Q$: $a = -10$. The Summer 2022 report names this slip too.
The free rise of 0.2 m is right, but it is added to where $Q$ started. While $P$ fell 0.8 m, $Q$ rose 0.8 m, so the free rise begins 1.6 m above the floor.
That is how much further $Q$ rises after the string goes slack. The question asks for its height above the floor, so add the 0.8 m it started at and the 0.8 m it rose while $P$ fell.

figures.alt: A car of 1200 kilograms towing a trailer of 400 kilograms along a horizontal road by a tow-bar.

parts.stem:
A car of mass 1200 kg tows a trailer of mass 400 kg along a straight horizontal road by a light horizontal tow-bar. The car's engine provides a driving force of 4100 N. Resistance to motion acts on each vehicle: 1.5 N for every kilogram of the car's mass and 0.75 N for every kilogram of the trailer's mass.

Show that the acceleration of the car and trailer is 1.25 m/s².

[3]

accepted: The resistances are 1800 N on the car and 300 N on the trailer. For the whole system, 4100 - 1800 - 300 = 1600a, so 2000 = 1600a and a = 1.25 m/s².

scheme.examinerNote: Substituting the printed value of a into the equation and checking both sides agree is verification, not a derivation, and CCEA caps that route at two marks.

hints: Convert each per-kilogram resistance first: each vehicle has its own rate.
The tow-bar's tension is internal to the pair, so the whole system is the quickest route here.
parts.workedSolution: The resistances are 1800 N on the car and 300 N on the trailer. For the whole system, 4100 - 1800 - 300 = 1600a, so 2000 = 1600a and a = 1.25 m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: Putting 1.25 into the equation and checking both sides agree is verification, not a derivation: CCEA caps that route at two of the three marks, and the mark it cannot reach is for forming the equation and solving it. Convert the resistances, form the equation and solve it forwards.
The rates per kilogram have been used as whole forces. Multiply each by its own vehicle's mass: 1.5 × 1200 = 1800 N on the car and 0.75 × 400 = 300 N on the trailer.

parts.stem:
Calculate the tension in the tow-bar.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: an equation of motion for one vehicle on its own

hints: The tension is internal to the pair, so the whole system cannot find it.
Use one vehicle on its own. For the trailer, only the tow-bar and its resistance act along its motion.
parts.workedSolution: For the trailer alone: $T - 300 = 400 \times 1.25 = 500$, so $T = 800$ N. The car's equation, $4100 - 1800 - T = 1200 \times 1.25$, gives the same.

commonErrors.feedback: That writes the trailer's equation with the car's mass and the car's resistance. Each equation carries only its own vehicle's numbers: for the trailer, $T - 300 = 400 \times 1.25$.
That is the trailer's resultant, $ma$, not the tension. The tow-bar also has to overcome the trailer's own resistance of 300 N.

parts.stem:
When the car and trailer are moving at 6 m/s, the tow-bar snaps. The resistance to the trailer's motion is unchanged.

Calculate the trailer's deceleration once the tow-bar has snapped.

Answer ________ m/s²

scheme.for: the trailer is now on its own, with no tension acting

hints: Redraw the trailer alone: the tow-bar is gone.
Only its resistance is left, acting backwards, so the trailer slows.
parts.workedSolution: With the tow-bar gone the only force along the trailer's motion is its resistance of 300 N, acting backwards: $-300 = 400a$, so $a = -0.75$ m/s² and the deceleration is $0.75$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That is the acceleration the pair had while the tow-bar held. The bar has snapped, so the force pulling the trailer forward is gone: redraw it and start again.
That divides the trailer's own resistance by the mass of both vehicles. They are separate bodies now, so only the trailer's mass belongs here.
Your working is right: with forwards positive, $a = -0.75$ m/s². The question asks for the deceleration, which is the size of that, so the answer is 0.75 m/s² with no minus sign.

parts.stem:
Calculate the distance the trailer travels after the tow-bar snaps, until it comes to rest.

Answer ________ m
hints: You know $u$, $v$ and $a$, and you want $s$: choose the formula without $t$.
With forwards positive, the deceleration goes in as a negative $a$.

commonErrors.feedback: That slows the trailer at 1.25 m/s², the acceleration the pair had while they were joined. After the snap its deceleration is the 0.75 m/s² from part (c).
That divides $u^2$ by $a$ instead of by $2a$. From $0 = u^2 + 2as$ with $a = -0.75$, $s = \frac{36}{1.5}$.

methodLock.instruction: Show that the acceleration of the car and trailer is 1.25 m/s²
methodLock.requiredMethod: Convert both resistances, form the equation of motion for the whole system (or for each vehicle, then add) and solve it for a; substituting the printed value back in is verification and is capped at two marks.

figures.alt: Block P, of mass M kilograms, on a horizontal table, joined by a string running over a pulley at the table's edge to block Q, 6 kilograms, hanging below.

parts.stem:
Block $P$, of mass $M$ kg, lies on a rough horizontal table. A light inextensible string joins it, over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table, to block $Q$, of mass 6 kg, which hangs freely. The friction on $P$ is 18 N. The blocks are released from rest, and 1.2 seconds later $Q$ has fallen 1.44 m. $P$ does not reach the pulley.

Calculate the acceleration of $P$ and $Q$.

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: The blocks start from rest, so $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$.
Square the time before you divide.
parts.workedSolution: From rest, $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$: $1.44 = \frac{1}{2} \times a \times 1.2^2$, so $1.44 = 0.72a$ and $a = 2$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: The time has not been squared. From rest, $1.44 = \frac{1}{2}a \times 1.2^2$, and $1.2^2$ is $1.44$.

parts.stem:
Calculate the tension in the string.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: $Q$ is the block whose mass you know: use its equation.
$Q$ accelerates downwards, so its weight comes first.
parts.workedSolution: For $Q$, down positive: $60 - T = 6 \times 2$, so $T = 48$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $Q$'s weight, the tension if $Q$ hung still. $Q$ is accelerating downwards, so the tension is less than its weight: $60 - T = 6a$.
That comes from $T - 60 = 6a$, with up as positive for a block that is accelerating down. Take $Q$'s own direction of travel: $60 - T = 6a$.

parts.stem:
Calculate the value of $M$.

Answer ________
hints: Now use $P$'s equation: along the table it has the tension forwards and friction backwards.
$P$'s weight and the normal reaction balance, so neither appears.

commonErrors.feedback: The friction is missing: $48 = 2M$ treats the tension as the whole resultant on $P$. The 18 N of friction acts against the motion, so $48 - 18 = 2M$.
That puts $P$'s weight, $10M$, into its equation along the table. $P$ moves horizontally, so its weight and the normal reaction balance and neither appears along the motion.

parts.stem:
The string runs horizontally from $P$ to the pulley and then vertically down to $Q$.

Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force the string exerts on the pulley.

Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: $R^2 = 48^2 + 48^2$: the two tensions act at a right angle

hints: Both sections pull on the pulley with the tension.
One section is horizontal and one vertical: draw the two pulls and combine them.
parts.workedSolution: The two pulls, each 48 N, are at a right angle, so $R^2 = 48^2 + 48^2$ and $R = 48\sqrt{2}$, which is $67.88$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That doubles the tension. $2T$ is right only when the two sections are parallel; here one is horizontal and one vertical, so the pulls combine by Pythagoras. The Summer 2025 report found most candidates doubling on this part.
That is one section's pull. The pulley is held by both sections, so it feels their resultant.

resources: Scientific calculator
Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

context.setting: Every force on the block on the table

figures.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 222' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='222'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='16' y='92' width='232' height='116' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.05'/><path d='M16 92H248V208' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><rect x='78' y='46' width='88' height='46' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='122' y='66' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>A</text><text x='122' y='84' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>6 kg</text><circle cx='268' cy='83' r='14' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><circle cx='268' cy='83' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M268 83L248 104' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><path d='M166 69L268 69' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><path d='M282 83L282 142' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><rect x='254' y='142' width='56' height='46' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='282' y='162' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>B</text><text x='282' y='180' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>4 kg</text></g></svg>
figures.alt: Block A, 6 kilograms, on a rough horizontal table, joined by a string over a pulley at the table's edge to block B, 4 kilograms, hanging below the pulley.

parts.stem:
Block $A$, of mass 6 kg, is on a rough horizontal table. A light inextensible string joins it, over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table, to block $B$, of mass 4 kg, which hangs freely and is falling.

Which list gives every force acting on $A$? Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________

options.text: Its weight of 60 N down, the normal reaction up, the tension towards the pulley and friction away from the pulley
options.feedback: Four forces, each with its direction: the weight and the reaction balance, and along the table the tension pulls towards the pulley while friction resists the motion.

options.text: Its weight of 60 N down, the normal reaction up, the tension towards the pulley, friction away from the pulley, and $B$'s weight of 40 N
options.feedback: $B$'s weight acts on $B$, not on $A$. It reaches $A$ only through the string, as the tension, so drawing it on $A$ as well counts it twice.

options.text: Its weight of 60 N down, the tension towards the pulley and friction away from the pulley
options.feedback: The normal reaction is missing. The table pushes up on $A$, and without that push nothing balances $A$'s weight.

options.text: Its weight of 60 N down, the normal reaction up, the tension towards the pulley and friction towards the pulley
options.feedback: Friction opposes the motion. $A$ moves towards the pulley, so friction points away from it.

scheme.for: weight down, normal reaction up, tension towards the pulley, friction away from it

hints: List the forces on $A$ alone: what touches it, and gravity.
Friction opposes the way $A$ moves.
parts.workedSolution: On $A$: its weight of 60 N down, the normal reaction from the table up, the tension along the string towards the pulley, and friction away from the pulley, against the motion. $B$'s weight acts on $B$.

resources: Scientific calculator
Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

context.setting: A pair that stays still

parts.stem:
Block $A$, of mass 5 kg, rests on a rough horizontal table. A light inextensible string joins it, over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table, to block $B$, of mass 2 kg, which hangs freely. Both blocks stay at rest.

Calculate the friction acting on $A$.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: $T = 20$ ($B$ is at rest, so the tension balances $B$'s weight)
$F = T$ ($A$ is at rest, so the forces along the table balance)

hints: Nothing moves, so there is no $ma$ anywhere: every pair of forces balances.
Start with $B$: what must the tension be to hold it still?
parts.workedSolution: $B$ is at rest, so $T = 2 \times 10 = 20$ N. $A$ is at rest too, so along the table the friction balances the tension: $F = 20$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $B$'s mass in kilograms. The balance $F = T$ is right, so that mark (M) stands; the tension holds up $B$'s weight, $2 \times 10 = 20$ N.
That is $A$'s own weight. It presses down into the table and the normal reaction balances it; along the table only the tension and the friction act, and they balance.
Friction does not need movement to act. The string is pulling $A$ towards the pulley with 20 N, and something must hold it back, or it would move: that is the friction.

findTheMistake.stem: Saoirse is finding the magnitude of the force on a pulley at the edge of a table. The string runs horizontally along the table, over the pulley, and vertically down, and the tension is 35 N. Her working:
studentWorking: The force on the pulley is the resultant of the two tensions
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 adds the two pulls as if they pointed the same way. They do not: one section is horizontal and the other vertical, so the pulls are at a right angle, and doubling works only when the sections are parallel. The two equal pulls make a square, and the resultant is its diagonal, at $45°$ to each section: $\sqrt{35^2 + 35^2} = 49.50$ N.
correction: The force on the pulley is the resultant of the two tensions
Each section pulls with 35 N, one horizontally and one vertically
findTheMistake.feedback: Line 1 is exactly the right principle; the method mark is for carrying it out, combining the two pulls by Pythagoras at a right angle. Draw the two pulls every time before reaching for a formula: doubling here is what most candidates did on the least well-answered part of the Summer 2025 paper.

findTheMistake.stem: Fionn is finding the acceleration of a 4 kg block on a rough horizontal table, joined over a smooth pulley at the edge to a 6 kg block hanging freely. The friction on the block on the table is 12 N. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 subtracts the weight of the block on the table, 40 N. That block moves horizontally, so its weight presses straight into the table and the normal reaction balances it exactly: neither force has any part along the motion. Only the hanging weight and the friction belong in this equation.
findTheMistake.feedback: Working with the whole system is a legitimate route to the acceleration, and the driving weight in line 2 is right; the extra term in line 3 is what costs the marks. Drawing each body's own diagram first protects against it: on the block on the table you would see the weight and the reaction cancel before anything reached the equation.

findTheMistake.stem: Méabh is finding the deceleration of a trailer after its tow-bar snaps. The trailer's mass is 250 kg, the resistance to its motion is 200 N, and before the snap the car and trailer accelerated at 1.2 m/s². Her working:
studentWorking: The trailer keeps the acceleration it had
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 carries the old acceleration across the snap. That acceleration came from the driving force reaching the trailer through the tow-bar, and the bar has gone. What is left along the trailer's motion is its resistance of 200 N, acting backwards, which now slows it.
correction: The tow-bar has snapped, so redraw the trailer on its own
findTheMistake.feedback: Noticing that the bar has snapped is the right starting point; the marks come from what follows it. Make the redraw an explicit step: new diagram, new equation, new acceleration. The Summer 2019 report records this as the part only the more able candidates managed.

prompts.prompt: What is the method for two connected bodies?
prompts.answer: One diagram and one equation for each body, with the same tension and the same acceleration, then add the two equations.

prompts.prompt: Why is the tension the same in both sections of the string?
prompts.answer: Because the string is light and the pulley is smooth.

prompts.prompt: Why do both bodies have the same magnitude of acceleration?
prompts.answer: Because the string is inextensible, so it cannot stretch and one body can only move as the other lets it.

prompts.prompt: What is the force a string exerts on a pulley?
prompts.answer: The resultant of the two tensions: the vector sum of the pulls from the two sections, found by drawing them and combining them.

prompts.prompt: When is the force on a pulley equal to $2T$?
prompts.answer: Only when the two sections of string are parallel, so both pulls point the same way.

prompts.prompt: What is the force on a pulley when one section is horizontal and the other vertical?
prompts.answer: T√2, that is T root two, from R² = T² + T², at 45° to each section.

prompts.prompt: A string breaks or goes slack, or a tow-bar snaps. What do you do next?
prompts.answer: Redraw each body on its own and start again: there is no tension now, and each body has its own acceleration. A block still moving upwards slows at 10 m/s².

prompts.prompt: Does the weight of a block sliding on a horizontal table appear in its equation of motion?
prompts.answer: No: it acts at right angles to the motion and the normal reaction balances it, though both still belong on the diagram.

prompts.prompt: Why can the whole system's equation never give the tension in a tow-bar?
prompts.answer: Because the tension is internal: the tow-bar pulls the trailer forward and the car back equally, so it cancels. Use one vehicle's own equation, the trailer's or the car's.

prompts.prompt: Which three arrangements of connected bodies does this specification set?
prompts.answer: Both moving horizontally, both moving vertically, or one horizontally and one vertically.

prompts.prompt: A question gives a time and a distance, or a speed, before any force. What do you find first?
prompts.answer: The acceleration, from a constant-acceleration formula; then one body's equation gives the tension, and the other body's gives the unknown.

prompts.prompt: A part asks you to show that a mass or a resistance has a given value. How do you treat it?
prompts.answer: Keep it as a letter in the equation of motion and solve for it; never use the given value before it has been shown, or in an earlier part.

prompts.prompt: A string breaks or goes slack, or a tow-bar snaps. What do you do next?
prompts.answer: Redraw each body on its own: there is no tension now, and each body has its own acceleration.

prompts.prompt: Why can the whole system's equation never give the tension in a tow-bar?
prompts.answer: The tension is internal: it pulls the trailer forward and the car back, so it cancels. Use one vehicle's own equation.

prompts.prompt: A part asks you to show that a mass or a resistance has a given value. How do you treat it?
prompts.answer: Keep it as a letter in the equation of motion and solve for it; never use the given value early.

findings.asked: Car and trailer: equations of motion, tension, then the car's new acceleration after the tow-bar breaks.
findings.wentWrong: Many could not write an equation for the trailer alone and tried the whole system or the car; arithmetic slips followed; the post-break acceleration was widely unattempted.
findings.rule: Write F = ma for each body separately; after a break, recompute the resultant force on what remains.

findings.asked: Two blocks over a pulley: diagram, equations, force on the pulley, later motion.
findings.wentWrong: Tension arrows wrong; g omitted; equations of motion poorly formed and badly solved simultaneously; many did not realise that, with both sections hanging vertically, the pulley carried twice the tension; the earlier acceleration was reused after the string went slack.
findings.rule: Force on a pulley = resultant of the two tensions (2T when the strings hang parallel); a free particle then moves under gravity alone.

findings.asked: Connected blocks: diagram, then equations for each.
findings.wentWrong: Normal reaction missing on one block; different labels for the same tension; weight labelled M; arrows missing; F = ma attempted where it was not needed.
findings.rule: One string, one T; write each block's equation in its own direction of motion.

findings.asked: Car towing: resistive force, 'show that' a mass, then motion after separation.
findings.wentWrong: Substituting the later value of M into part (i) got zero; verifying by substitution got at most two marks; some used the car's motion for the trailer part.
findings.rule: Derive, do not verify; after separation each body has its own resultant force.

findings.asked: Two blocks and a pulley: diagram, acceleration, tension, force on the pulley.
findings.wentWrong: Treating the masses separately worked better than the whole system; equations mixed weights and masses; the force on the pulley was assumed to be 2T when the string geometry made it a different resultant — the least well answered item on the paper.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Found T, then added the two tension vectors along the string directions to get the magnitude of the force on the pulley.
findings.rule: The pulley feels the vector sum of the two tensions; 2T only if the string sections are parallel.

insight.ruleToRemember: Write F = ma for each particle in its direction of motion with the same T and a; the force on the pulley is the resultant of the two tensions (2T only when the strings are parallel); after a string breaks or a tow-bar snaps, recalculate the acceleration from the forces that remain.
insight.aStarSignal: Computing the force on a pulley whose strings are not parallel, and handling the motion after a connection breaks.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-b before writing)
checks.detail: g = 10 m/s²; every system solved once and the solution checked against BOTH of its equations by the generator. Vertical pair 5/3 kg: a = 2.5, T = 37.5, force on the pulley 2T = 75; released 0.8 m above the floor, the heavier lands at 2 m/s, the string goes slack and the lighter rises a further 0.2 m to 1.8 m above the floor. Table pair 7/5 kg with friction 14 N: a = 3, T = 35, force on the pulley T root 2 = 49.4974746831 printed 49.50. Tow-bar 1200/400 kg, drive 4100 N, 1.5 and 0.75 N per kg: resistances 1800 and 300, a = 1.25, tow-bar tension 800, trailer deceleration after the snap 0.75, and from 6 m/s it stops in 24 m. Practice: 6/4 kg gives a = 2, T = 48, pulley 96; 50 N at a right angle gives 70.71; 3/2 kg smooth gives a = 4, T = 12 and a pulley force of 16.97; 2/3 kg smooth gives a = 6, T = 12; 5/5 kg with 10 N friction gives a = 4, T = 30; 1000/500 kg with 1 N per kg gives a = 2, T = 1500, then 1 m/s² deceleration; a 3 m/s break gives 0.45 m. Find-the-mistake: 4/6 kg with 12 N friction gives a = 4.8 (the extra weight term gives 0.8); a 250 kg trailer with 200 N resistance decelerates at 0.8 (the old 1.2 is the error). Added 23 Sep 2026: rungs 6 kg at rest gives T = 60 and 4 kg lowered at 2 m/s² gives T = 32; the timed table pair (exam-style q.0020) from rest over 1.44 m in 1.2 s gives a = 2, then T = 48, M = 15 and a pulley force of 67.88, checked in the combined equation; worked example 4, 1500/480 kg with 2766 N and k and 2k N per kg at 0.9 m/s², gives k = 0.4 from the whole system, T = 816 (checked in the car's equation), a deceleration of 0.8 after the break and 9 s to rest from 7.2 m/s, twin T = 740; the note's run-on car, 1000/600 kg at 0.8 N per kg with 3200 N, gives a = 1.2, 12 m/s after 10 s, then 2.4 m/s² alone and 24 m/s 5 s later; gates g8 4, g9 850, g10 0.8, g13 2.5. Added 24 Sep 2026, the tail-only items: q.0021 lists the forces on a 6 kg block on the table (weight 60 N; the distractor's extra force is the 4 kg block's weight, 40 N); q.0022 holds a 5 kg block and a 2 kg block at rest, so T = 20 N and the friction is 20 N (its errors: 2, the mass; 50, the table block's weight; 0, friction left out). No set of masses, forces or speeds here is taken from a CCEA paper: the Summer 2025 Q4 table pair and the Summer 2024 Q6 car mass were replaced on 22 Sep 2026. The tow-bar car's 1200 kg equals the Summer 2026 car's mass by coincidence; its trailer, driving force, resistances and acceleration all differ.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-b before writing)
checks.detail: All five findings on packs/further-maths/insights/u2.connected-particles-and-pulleys.json are exercised, read against the Chief Examiner's reports for Summer 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, with the Summer 2021 and 2026 papers read for their shapes (2021 has a scheme but no report). The note (23 Sep 2026 depth pass) has an idea, a why and an arrangements section, six variants each with worked lines (both hanging, table, car and trailer, the pulley, the slack string, the broken tow-bar), a derivation of T root 2, six twists from the papers in frequency order, and a going-further chain from Summer 2019 Q5(iv). Summer 2025 Q4(iv), the least well-answered item on that paper, drives sections 7 and 8 (with the body's one examiner callout), gates g3 and g4, diagnostics 07, 08 and 09, practice 4 and 5, find-the-mistake 01 and the pulley parts of two exam-style questions; the table block's weight carried into its equation (the report's own named error) drives diagnostic 11, practice 7 and 9, find-the-mistake 02 and exam-style 1(a). Summer 2022 Q5 (the pulley force not known to be 2T; the part (ii) acceleration or +10 used once the string went slack) drives section 9, gate g5, practice 3 and 14, and exam-style question 2, whose last part is the slack string; the timing-first shape of Summer 2021 Q4 and Summer 2023 Q4 drives the twists, gate g12, rp.11 and exam-style q.0020; the later value used early (Summer 2024 Q6) drives gate g11 and rp.12. Summer 2019 Q5 and Summer 2024 Q6 (an equation for the whole system or the car where the trailer was needed; a later printed value used in an earlier part; the post-break parts) drive diagnostics 10 and 12, find-the-mistake 03, practice 10 and 11 and exam-style question 3. Summer 2023 Q4 (one string, one T; the normal reaction missing; the wrong body's mass) drives sections 1 and 2, gates g1 and g7 and diagnostics 05 and 06. The dossier's split diagram and its pulley parallelograms are rebuilt as our own figures. The dossier's photograph was dropped after inspection: it shows a block and tackle whose hanging block sits on two strands, not the one-string arrangement it would have illustrated.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-b before writing)
checks.detail: Every inline SVG carries a viewBox, draws in currentColor, is under 12 KB and contains no style element, script, event handler, href or prefers-color-scheme rule, and no hash or percent sign. Every figure is drawn by scratchpad/fm2-batch-d/fig.mjs (pairFig, tableFig, towFig, pullsFig, splitFig, arrangementsFig, bodyFig) in a 400-unit viewBox with 14- and 15-unit labels, at least 12.5 px on a 358 px phone column; the builder throws when a label falls under the floor, when two labels overlap, or when a marker leaves the viewBox. The right-angle pulley figure draws the two pulls from the axle and the resultant as the diagonal of the square they build, so the picture and the arithmetic cannot disagree. The note has the annotated copies; worked examples and questions have plain copies with the given masses and no forces.

checks.tool: claude (FM2 batch D, fourth session: teach before you check)
checks.detail: Read end to end as the student under the owner's ruling of 24 Sep 2026 (teach, then show, then check). Section 1 shows one pair's equations added before gate g1 asks for another; section 2 points the cancelling at those lines; section 7 shows 2T worked; the twists show an unknown mass kept as a letter and an acceleration found from a timing before gates g11 and g12; every gate's explanation re-teaches before the answer. The note's demonstrations take numbers no item uses: the 23 Sep note solved exam-style q.0015 (7 kg table pair), q.0016 (5 kg and 3 kg from 0.8 m, with that question's own figure) and q.0017 (1200 kg car) in front of her, and gate g1 was the pre-diagnostic's own question; now 9/3 kg, 8/2 kg (from 0.9 m), 3 kg on the table with 7 kg hanging against 9 N, and an 1100 kg car with a 300 kg trailer. Two short prompts are embedded.

checks.detail: g = 10 m/s²; every system solved once and the solution checked against BOTH of its equations by the generator. Vertical pair 5/3 kg: a = 2.5, T = 37.5, force on the pulley 2T = 75; released 0.8 m above the floor, the heavier lands at 2 m/s, the string goes slack and the lighter rises a further 0.2 m to 1.8 m above the floor. Table pair 7/5 kg with friction 14 N: a = 3, T = 35, force on the pulley T root 2 = 49.4974746831 printed 49.50. Tow-bar 1200/400 kg, drive 4100 N, 1.5 and 0.75 N per kg: resistances 1800 and 300, a = 1.25, tow-bar tension 800, trailer deceleration after the snap 0.75, and from 6 m/s it stops in 24 m. Practice: 6/4 kg gives a = 2, T = 48, pulley 96; 50 N at a right angle gives 70.71; 3/2 kg smooth gives a = 4, T = 12 and a pulley force of 16.97; 2/3 kg smooth gives a = 6, T = 12; 5/5 kg with 10 N friction gives a = 4, T = 30; 1000/500 kg with 1 N per kg gives a = 2, T = 1500, then 1 m/s² deceleration; a 3 m/s break gives 0.45 m. Find-the-mistake: 4/6 kg with 12 N friction gives a = 4.8 (the extra weight term gives 0.8); a 250 kg trailer with 200 N resistance decelerates at 0.8 (the old 1.2 is the error). Added 24 Sep 2026, the tail-only items: q.0021 lists the forces on a 6 kg block on the table (weight 60 N; the distractor's extra force is the 4 kg block's weight, 40 N); q.0022 holds a 5 kg block and a 2 kg block at rest, so T = 20 N and the friction is 20 N (its errors: 2, the mass; 50, the table block's weight; 0, friction left out). checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-b before writing)
checks.detail: g = 10 m/s²; every system solved once and the solution checked against BOTH of its equations by the generator. Vertical pair 5/3 kg: a = 2.5, T = 37.5, force on the pulley 2T = 75; released 0.8 m above the floor, the heavier lands at 2 m/s, the string goes slack and the lighter rises a further 0.2 m to 1.8 m above the floor. Table pair 7/5 kg with friction 14 N: a = 3, T = 35, force on the pulley T root 2 = 49.4974746831 printed 49.50. Tow-bar 1200/400 kg, drive 4100 N, 1.5 and 0.75 N per kg: resistances 1800 and 300, a = 1.25, tow-bar tension 800, trailer deceleration after the snap 0.75, and from 6 m/s it stops in 24 m. Practice: 6/4 kg gives a = 2, T = 48, pulley 96; 50 N at a right angle gives 70.71; 3/2 kg smooth gives a = 4, T = 12 and a pulley force of 16.97; 2/3 kg smooth gives a = 6, T = 12; 5/5 kg with 10 N friction gives a = 4, T = 30; 1000/500 kg with 1 N per kg gives a = 2, T = 1500, then 1 m/s² deceleration; a 3 m/s break gives 0.45 m. Find-the-mistake: 4/6 kg with 12 N friction gives a = 4.8 (the extra weight term gives 0.8); a 250 kg trailer with 200 N resistance decelerates at 0.8 (the old 1.2 is the error). Added 23 Sep 2026: rungs 6 kg at rest gives T = 60 and 4 kg lowered at 2 m/s² gives T = 32; the timed table pair (exam-style q.0020) from rest over 1.44 m in 1.2 s gives a = 2, then T = 48, M = 15 and a pulley force of 67.88, checked in the combined equation; worked example 4, 1500/480 kg with 2766 N and k and 2k N per kg at 0.9 m/s², gives k = 0.4 from the whole system, T = 816 (checked in the car's equation), a deceleration of 0.8 after the break and 9 s to rest from 7.2 m/s, twin T = 740; the note's run-on car, 1000/600 kg at 0.8 N per kg with 3200 N, gives a = 1.2, 12 m/s after 10 s, then 2.4 m/s² alone and 24 m/s 5 s later; gates g8 4, g9 850, g10 0.8, g13 2.5. Added 24 Sep 2026, the tail-only items: q.0021 lists the forces on a 6 kg block on the table (weight 60 N; the distractor's extra force is the 4 kg block's weight, 40 N); q.0022 holds a 5 kg block and a 2 kg block at rest, so T = 20 N and the friction is 20 N (its errors: 2, the mass; 50, the table block's weight; 0, friction left out). No set of masses, forces or speeds here is taken from a CCEA paper: the Summer 2025 Q4 table pair and the Summer 2024 Q6 car mass were replaced on 22 Sep 2026. The tow-bar car's 1200 kg equals the Summer 2026 car's mass by coincidence; its trailer, driving force, resistances and acceleration all differ.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-b before writing)
checks.detail: g = 10 m/s²; every system solved once and the solution checked against BOTH of its equations by the generator. Vertical pair 5/3 kg: a = 2.5, T = 37.5, force on the pulley 2T = 75; released 0.8 m above the floor, the heavier lands at 2 m/s, the string goes slack and the lighter rises a further 0.2 m to 1.8 m above the floor. Table pair 7/5 kg with friction 14 N: a = 3, T = 35, force on the pulley T root 2 = 49.4974746831 printed 49.50. Tow-bar 1200/400 kg, drive 4100 N, 1.5 and 0.75 N per kg: resistances 1800 and 300, a = 1.25, tow-bar tension 800, trailer deceleration after the snap 0.75, and from 6 m/s it stops in 24 m. Practice: 6/4 kg gives a = 2, T = 48, pulley 96; 50 N at a right angle gives 70.71; 3/2 kg smooth gives a = 4, T = 12 and a pulley force of 16.97; 2/3 kg smooth gives a = 6, T = 12; 5/5 kg with 10 N friction gives a = 4, T = 30; 1000/500 kg with 1 N per kg gives a = 2, T = 1500, then 1 m/s² deceleration; a 3 m/s break gives 0.45 m. Find-the-mistake: 4/6 kg with 12 N friction gives a = 4.8 (the extra weight term gives 0.8); a 250 kg trailer with 200 N resistance decelerates at 0.8 (the old 1.2 is the error). Added 23 Sep 2026: rungs 6 kg at rest gives T = 60 and 4 kg lowered at 2 m/s² gives T = 32; the timed table pair (exam-style q.0020) from rest over 1.44 m in 1.2 s gives a = 2, then T = 48, M = 15 and a pulley force of 67.88, checked in the combined equation; worked example 4, 1500/480 kg with 2766 N and k and 2k N per kg at 0.9 m/s², gives k = 0.4 from the whole system, T = 816 (checked in the car's equation), a deceleration of 0.8 after the break and 9 s to rest from 7.2 m/s, twin T = 740; the note's run-on car, 1000/600 kg at 0.8 N per kg with 3200 N, gives a = 1.2, 12 m/s after 10 s, then 2.4 m/s² alone and 24 m/s 5 s later; gates g8 4, g9 850, g10 0.8, g13 2.5. Added 24 Sep 2026, the tail-only items: q.0021 lists the forces on a 6 kg block on the table (weight 60 N; the distractor's extra force is the 4 kg block's weight, 40 N); q.0022 holds a 5 kg block and a 2 kg block at rest, so T = 20 N and the friction is 20 N (its errors: 2, the mass; 50, the table block's weight; 0, friction left out). No set of masses, forces or speeds here is taken from a CCEA paper: the Summer 2025 Q4 table pair and the Summer 2024 Q6 car mass were replaced on 22 Sep 2026. The tow-bar car's 1200 kg equals the Summer 2026 car's mass by coincidence; its trailer, driving force, resistances and acceleration all differ.
